title: The Great Amen and the Our Father
word: The Great Amen and the Our Fathe
hook: the whole church says one loud Amen, then his own prayer
carry: so be it, all of us

segments.voice: Yesterday, the consecration, and the long word transubstantiation. Your line was this is my body. Did you keep three seconds of silence before a meal? Day one hundred and fifteen.

In the generations after the apostles, a Christian teacher in Rome named Justin wrote a defense of the faith addressed to the emperor. People were spreading rumors about what Christians did at their secret gatherings, and he wanted to set the record straight. So he described a Sunday. They meet, he wrote. They read from the apostles and the prophets. Someone preaches. They pray. Bread and wine and water are brought. The one presiding gives thanks at length. And then, Justin says, all the people present answer with one word. He even explains the word for the emperor, because it wasn't Greek or Latin. It was Hebrew, and it meant: so be it. Today, that word, and the prayer that follows.
screen: `JUSTIN, IN ROME.` → `A LETTER TO THE EMPEROR.` → `ALL THE PEOPLE, ONE WORD.`

segments.voice: The word is Amen. It comes from a Hebrew root meaning firm, solid, reliable. At Mass, the long prayer over the bread and wine ends with the priest lifting both high, the bread and the cup together, and singing that through Christ, with him and in him, all glory and honor belong to the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit. In Latin, Per ipsum, et cum ipso, et in ipso. And the whole church answers: Amen. It's called the Great Amen, and it's often sung, sometimes repeated. It's the people's signature on everything the priest has just prayed. Saint Jerome wrote that in Rome the Amen boomed out like thunder from heaven. Then, straight after, everyone stands and prays the Our Father together. In the Douay-Rheims it opens: "Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name." It's the prayer Jesus taught his friends, and it's here for a reason. It asks for daily bread, just before the bread is shared. It asks to forgive, just before the sign of peace. At Mass, one thing is different. After deliver us from evil, the priest keeps going with a short prayer for peace and freedom from anxiety. Then everyone ends together, giving God the kingdom, the power and the glory, now and forever. Some churches say that line straight after the prayer. At Mass, it comes here. First a whole church signs its name. Then it prays like a family.
screen: `AMEN: FIRM, SO BE IT.` · `THROUGH HIM, WITH HIM, IN HIM.` · `AN AMEN LIKE THUNDER.` · `THEN THE PRAYER HE TAUGHT.` · then, large: `OUR FATHER WHO ART IN HEAVEN, HALLOWED BE THY NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one amen, meant. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you agree with deep down. A hope for someone. A thing you know is true. Something good you want to happen. Hold it clearly. Then, if you pray, say amen, out loud if you can, like a signature, not a murmur. If you don't pray, say yes to it instead, firmly. Notice the difference between agreeing and signing. Then sit. The bell holds the time.
The Great Amen and the Our Father. The people's loud so be it to the whole prayer of the Mass, then the prayer Jesus taught, said together. Today's word.
screen: `THE GREAT AMEN AND THE OUR FATHER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: so be it, all of us. Today, when a group decides something good, a plan, a toast, a promise, be the one who says yes out loud. Day one hundred and fifteen.

howItsDone: At the end of the Eucharistic Prayer the priest raises the consecrated bread and chalice and the congregation responds with the Great Amen, often sung; then all stand to pray the Lord's Prayer, followed by the priest's prayer for peace and the people's closing doxology.

trapdoor: what you thought: amen means the prayer is over.
what it means: the whole church's signature, so be it, on the great prayer, then the family prayer Jesus taught.

what a scholar hears: Justin's First Apology 65 records the people's Amen and glosses the Hebrew word for the emperor; the Mass places the closing doxology after the embolism, the priest's prayer for peace.

notes: The index word is truncated ('The Great Amen and the Our Fathe'); kept exactly as the validator requires. The index should be corrected to 'The Great Amen and the Our Father' in a separate, owner-approved edit.
Douay-Rheims Matthew 6:9 given from memory; confirm.
Justin, First Apology 65: the people's Amen and his explanation that it means 'so be it' in Hebrew; paraphrased. Confirm.
Jerome's image of the Amen resounding like heavenly thunder (Commentary on Galatians, book 2, preface): widely cited; confirm the source.
The final doxology, the embolism ('deliver us, Lord…'), and the people's acclamation are paraphrased, not quoted from ICEL.
The doxology 'for thine is the kingdom…' is absent from the earliest manuscripts of Matthew and appears in the Didache; confirm the trapdoor wording.

Editor review (2026-10-01): removed dates the cited texts don't state (Justin 'around 155', Jerome 'around 400'; the Commentary on Galatians is usually dated c. 386), the 'three or more times' count, the superlative 'the one prayer Jesus taught', the 'many churches' claim and the trapdoor's manuscript claim; the closing doxology is now described rather than echoing the ICEL wording.
